title: Quincy under pressure, Aretha's green dress and Quincy's reply to traditionalists
summary: Quincy looked exhausted on a weekend deadline; Aretha's unexpected green dress upset Peggy Lee; Quincy answered complaints about repertoire.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: Yeah. Well, Quincy almost went under. We were at the Tandem Enterprises. that's Bud Yorkin and Norman Lear, you know? We met there about 11:00 o'clock on a Friday night, and Sunday we had to do like wall to wall music. Now, you're involved in copyists, weekends, and you know it's a tough

situation. Quincy was late. We were all there early. It was just Fillmore, Luther Henderson, Bud Yorkin and all the secretaries, sitting there, just waiting. Quincy came in there looking green. When you mentioned that -- when you said the color green, I was worried about Quincy then. Because he's had -- his eyes were almost as baggy as Duke's, you know. It was just a tremendous thing to take on.
Yeah. It was a tremendous thing to take on. You have to fight with the networks and fight with the time, and --
And worry about artists and their temperaments.

Oh, that was funny. Well, you know who cracked up about it. Now we sat there, and Harris, the guy that's got the Midnight Special Show, the producer, he says, 'Now, what we are going to do is have black dresses, like black velvet, that kind of thing, and we'll superimpose with the trombones, which will be gold, which makes a great combination.' And this is a funny story. It went down. The dress rehearsal went down just like that until the show time, and Aretha put that green dress on.
Yes, and it just -- and Peggy Lee went

into a gorilla bag, really. She said, "Didn't you tell us you were going to wear the same thing we were going to wear?" So then I went into the back and Quincy went into the back and said, "Oh, no, I don't want to hear all this."

Yeah, it was really funny. And -- but it -- all in all it turned out good, because there was some -- I think Quincy had a classic answer. A lot of people were saying they were traditionalists, you know, and they were saying, well why -- they wanted to hear like, "Black, Brown and Beige," and these kinds of things. Well, those eras have gotten away from him -- from us, really. And they've been documented, however. And Quincy would say, "Well if you loved Duke so much why didn't you do it?" And that stopped all the big conversation. And the man was -- he was very sick then.
Yeah, he was a sick man, on his way, you know. But he did get under the wire. They gave him a good tribute, you know, to Americana, which he richly deserved.
